\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Long-Term Structural Health Monitoring of a Cable-Stayed Bridge\\Under Operational and Environmental Loads}
\author{J.~Lindqvist, A.~Mbeki, and R.~Tanaka}
\date{June 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
This paper reports on four years of continuous structural health
monitoring of a 640~m cable-stayed bridge carrying both road and light
rail traffic. A dense array of accelerometers, strain gauges, and
environmental sensors recorded more than nine terabytes of time series
between 2022 and 2025. We describe the monitoring campaign, present the
identified modal parameters and their seasonal variation, and show that
temperature-induced changes in the first vertical bending frequency
reach 6\%, exceeding the changes attributable to traffic loading by an
order of magnitude. The dataset is released to support benchmarking of
damage-detection algorithms under realistic environmental variability.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Long-span bridges are among the most heavily instrumented civil
structures, and the case for instrumenting them is straightforward: the
cost of an unexpected closure dwarfs the cost of a monitoring system,
and early detection of stiffness loss can extend service life by
decades. Yet the promise of damage detection based on vibration
monitoring remains only partly realised, largely because environmental
variability masks the subtle signatures of damage in the modal
parameters that most algorithms track.

The confounding role of temperature has been recognised for two decades,
but quantitative models of the temperature--frequency relationship are
still largely bridge-specific, and the community lacks long, openly
available records in which environmental and operational conditions are
logged with the same care as the structural response itself. The
monitoring campaign described here was designed from the outset to close
this gap: every structural sensor is paired with environmental channels,
and the data pipeline preserves raw time series alongside the identified
modal quantities.

The contributions of the paper are threefold. First, we document a
four-year monitoring campaign on a major cable-stayed bridge in full
engineering detail. Second, we quantify the seasonal and diurnal
variation of the first eight modal frequencies and attribute it to
specific environmental drivers. Third, we release the complete dataset
together with the processing chain, so that damage-detection methods can
be benchmarked against realistic, uncurated variability.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes
the bridge and the instrumentation. Section 3 presents the monitoring
campaign in detail. Section 4 reports the identified modal parameters
and their environmental modulation, Section 5 discusses implications for
damage detection, and Section 6 concludes.

\section{Bridge and Instrumentation}
The monitored structure is a cable-stayed bridge with a main span of
340~m and two side spans of 150~m each, opened to traffic in 2009. The
deck is a steel-concrete composite box girder carrying four road lanes
and two light rail tracks. The two pylons rise 118~m above the deck, and
the stay cables are arranged in a semi-fan configuration with 22 pairs
per pylon.

The instrumentation was specified jointly by the bridge authority and
the research consortium, with the explicit goal that environmental
channels should match structural channels in number and in quality. The
full sensor layout is presented in Section 3.2. The data acquisition
system samples all channels synchronously, and the timing error between
the most distant nodes is kept below one millisecond by a dedicated
clock distribution network.

Three design decisions shaped the installation. First, all sensors were
selected for a ten-year service life with in-place calibration, because
lane closures for maintenance are restricted to four nights per year.
Second, the cable forces are monitored indirectly through vibration
measurements on each stay, avoiding the drift problems of load cells.
Third, the raw time series are retained rather than only spectral
summaries, which roughly doubles the storage cost but preserves the
option of reprocessing with future algorithms.

\section{Monitoring Campaign}
This section describes the four-year campaign in operational detail.

\subsection{Campaign Timeline}
The installation began in March 2022 with the pylon sensors and
proceeded deck segment by deck segment, so that partial coverage was
available from June 2022 onward. Full coverage was reached in November
2022, and the analysis period used in this paper runs from December 2022
to December 2025, omitting the commissioning phase. Planned outages for
maintenance totalled eleven days over the three years, and unplanned
outages, mostly caused by a failing network switch in the south pylon,
totalled a further six days.

\subsection{Sensor Layout}
The structural array comprises 48 accelerometers on the deck, 12 on the
two pylons, and 44 vibration pickups on the stays, together with 36
strain gauges welded to the box girder at six cross-sections. The deck
accelerometers are spaced at 17~m on both edges of the deck, which
resolves the first twelve vertical and torsional modes with a spatial
aliasing limit well above the frequency band of interest. Displacement
of the deck mid-span is tracked by two robotic total stations aimed at
prisms on the girder, providing an independent quasi-static channel that
anchors the double integration of the acceleration records.

The accelerometer positions were chosen by a modal-kinetic-energy
criterion evaluated on the finite element model of the bridge, subject
to the constraint that all deck sensors be reachable from the existing
maintenance walkways. The stay pickups are clamped two metres above the
deck anchorages, high enough to avoid spray from the road surface and
low enough to be serviced from a small aerial platform without closing
the rail tracks.

\subsection{Data Acquisition}
All channels are sampled at 200~Hz with 24-bit resolution, and the
acquisition nodes timestamp each sample against the distributed clock.
Data are transmitted over a fibre ring to the control room, where they
are written to redundant storage in one-hour segments. A watchdog
process verifies segment completeness every ten minutes and pages the
on-call engineer when any node misses three consecutive checks. The
modal identification runs nightly on the previous day's data using an
automated covariance-driven stochastic subspace implementation, and its
results are archived with full provenance metadata.

\subsection{Environmental Logging}
The environmental array comprises 28 temperature sensors distributed
through the box girder and on the stay cables, six anemometers at deck
and pylon heights, two pyranometers, a precipitation gauge, and four
humidity probes inside the box girder. The temperature sensors inside
the girder are paired at the top and bottom flanges, so that the
vertical thermal gradient that drives the daily curvature cycle can be
resolved directly rather than inferred from air temperature alone. Wind
records are quality-controlled against the bridge authority's separate
meteorological mast, and the two systems agree within 0.4~m/s on the
hourly means.

\subsection{Data Quality Screening}
Every channel passes through an automated screening chain that flags
spikes, dropouts, drift, and quantization faults against channel-specific
thresholds learned during commissioning. On average 1.8\% of
channel-hours are flagged each month, concentrated in the strain gauges
after lightning storms and in the total stations during heavy rain.
Flagged segments are never discarded silently: they are excluded from
the modal identification but retained in the archive with the flag
metadata, so that users of the dataset can apply their own trade-off
between coverage and quality.

\section{Results}
The first eight identified modal frequencies range from 0.41~Hz for the
first vertical bending mode to 4.9~Hz for the third torsional mode, and
all eight are tracked successfully on more than 97\% of the days in the
analysis period. The damping ratios identified by the subspace method
average 0.6\% for the vertical modes and 0.9\% for the torsional modes,
in line with values reported for comparable bridges.

The dominant source of modal variability is thermal. The first vertical
bending frequency varies by 6\% between the coldest and warmest weeks of
the record, and a hysteresis loop against air temperature collapses onto
a single curve when plotted against the deck gradient temperature
instead. As Section 3.2 explains, the accelerometers are clamped in
rigid brackets, which rules out sensor mounting effects as the origin of
the loop and supports the interpretation in terms of bearing restraint
and girder curvature.

A weekly periodicity is visible in the identified damping ratios of the
vertical modes, with weekend values about 15\% higher than weekday
values. We attribute this to the changed composition of traffic rather
than to any structural cause: the share of heavy rail vehicles falls on
weekends, and the lighter, more uniform road traffic excites the deck
more coherently, which biases the subspace estimator toward higher
apparent damping.

Traffic loading is the second driver but a much weaker one: the
frequency reduction between the quietest nights and the heaviest
commute peaks is below 0.6\% for all eight modes. The temperature
compensation follows Section 3.4, and after compensation the residual
variability of the first bending frequency drops from 6\% to 0.7\%,
which defines the noise floor against which any damage index must be
evaluated on this structure.

\section{Discussion}
The results quantify, for this bridge, the well-known warning that
environmental compensation is not an optional refinement but a
prerequisite for damage detection: an uncompensated detector would raise
seasonal false alarms with an amplitude ten times the residual noise
floor. The released dataset, with its paired environmental channels, is
intended to let other groups test their compensation and detection
methods without the multi-year negotiation that usually precedes access
to bridge monitoring data.

Two limitations deserve emphasis. The record covers three full winters
and is therefore informative about seasonal but not about decadal
variability, and the structure suffered no known damage during the
period, so the dataset benchmarks false-alarm behaviour but not
detection power.

\section{Conclusion}
We have documented a four-year structural health monitoring campaign on
a cable-stayed bridge, from the sensor layout and acquisition chain to
the identified modal parameters and their environmental drivers. The
headline numbers are stark: thermal effects move the first bending
frequency by 6\%, traffic by less than 0.6\%, and compensation reduces
the residual to 0.7\%. The complete dataset and processing chain are
released to the community. Future work will use the record to develop
transferable temperature models and to test damage-detection algorithms
under controlled injection of synthetic stiffness loss.
\end{document}
